summary: Intro demo to Redwood Hosted API for Lumenly focused on real-time chat generation. transcript:
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, um we're gonna run through a pretty focused 30ish minute demo on hosted chat gen then leave time for q's. Ethan will drive the demo.
[00:12] Ethan: hi. i'll share my screen, give me a sec. so the core idea is streaming lets you start sending tokens to the client as they're generated — reduces time-to-first-byte. we show both streaming and non-streaming endpoints.
[00:28] Tomás: quick question, are streaming payloads charged differently?
[00:33] Maya: good call. pricing is per-token for generation and for embeddings separately; streaming doesn't change billing it's still token-based but you can reduce perceived latency. also Console will show token counts per request so you can see unit economics.
[00:46] Priya: ok, and how do we control length and randomness? we have a lot of short prompts and some long summaries.
[00:53] Ethan: a few params — max_tokens caps generation length. temperature controls randomness; low temps deterministic, high temps more creative. top_p is nucleus sampling. stop sequences end generation early — good for structured outputs. i usually demo 3 examples.
[01:10] Ethan: (shares code) here's a streaming example, we open a websocket, send messages and get partial chunks. note that the SDK returns "delta" chunks and you can assemble them client-side.
[01:26] Aisha: is there a canonical way to merge partial deltas? we saw weird partial tokens once, like words split.
[01:33] Ethan: yeah words can be split across chunks. recommended pattern: append chunks to a buffer and only render completed sub-tokens if you're doing token-level display, or render progressively but be ready to patch. also we expose an 'is_final' flag on the final chunk for convenience in the SDK.
[01:50] Tomás: what about retries — if we do an automatic retry on a 5xx are we gonna double charge?
[01:57] Ethan: good, two parts here — idempotency and server side dedupe. Redwood supports client-provided idempotency-key header. if you retry with same key and the initial request reached the model we dedupe so tokens won't be generated twice. if the request never reached model (gateway failure) then retry is safe. we also recommend exponential backoff with jitter: start 200ms, double, cap at 2s plus random jitter.
[02:18] Priya: is idempotency-key required?
[02:20] Ethan: not required, but recommended for at-least-once network retries. SDKs add it by default for critical flows.
[02:28] Maya: to add, Console will show request traces including idempotency keys so you can audit what happened.
[02:35] Ethan: demo time — Example 1: short reply, max_tokens 40, temp 0.2. streaming latency ~120ms to first token in our sandbox. Example 2: longer summary, max_tokens 400, temp 0.6. you can see token accumulation in Console.
[03:02] Ethan: Example 3 we show stop sequences — we ask model to produce YAML and include --- as stop. that prevents model from continuing.
[03:15] Tomás: regarding batching — we do many small parallel chats, is batch size something you tune?
[03:21] Ethan: yes, batching at the server reduces per-token cost but can increase tail latency. Optimize (the product) suggests batching config per route based on your latency SLO and request size distribution. Console will also show batching utilization. typical advice: for synchronous chat low-latency apps, keep batching small, e.g., 4-8; for background jobs increase to 32+.
[03:44] Priya: you mentioned quantized models earlier?
[03:47] Ethan: right. we host multiple model variants — full fp16, int8/4 quantized variants. quant reduces VRAM and cost, sometimes with small quality regressions. Optimize will recommend a quant profile per workload; we also provide AB rollouts so you can compare outputs side-by-side in Console.
[04:05] Aisha: and if one variant is down or overloaded?
[04:08] Ethan: smart routing — requests can fallback to compatible variants or different regions. fallback rules are configurable per route; e.g., prefer int8 but fallback to fp16 if latency gets high.
[04:19] Maya: security quick note — we support API keys, optional VPC peering for Private, KMS integrations for Bring-Your-Own-Key in Private deployments.
[04:30] Priya: we have strict data residency — EU only. do you have region pinning?
[04:33] Ethan: yes, you can pin to EU, and Private gives full control. for Hosted we have EU regions and we can enable customer region routing.
[04:43] Tomás: can you show Console trace for a failed request and how to troubleshoot?
[04:47] Ethan: ssh, i mean sure — opening Console. here's a request trace — you can see transport failure, then the retry attempts, then the idempotency key showing dedupe. token estimator shows an estimate pre-request and actual tokens after.
[05:09] Ethan: note, occasionally transcriber note: some brand names might appear garbled in the recording, 'KV cache' could be transcribed as 'KV cash' — ignore that.
[05:20] Priya: what's the typical retry pattern you ship in SDKs?
[05:23] Ethan: SDKs implement exponential backoff with full jitter, 3 retries by default for transient 5xx + network timeouts. for 429 rate-limits we recommend token-bucket client-side and backoff with retry-after header honoring.
[05:36] Tomás: how do you handle partial generations on retry? like if client disconnected mid-stream then reconnects and retries?
[05:44] Ethan: if you use the same idempotency key, Redwood will return the last completed result if it finished, or resume semantic? currently we don't stream resume mid-token; we return the final output for a completed run. for long-running streaming sessions we suggest checkpoints client-side and application-level resume tokens.
[06:04] Maya: switching to cost controls — Console allows per-route quotas, soft-limits, and token burn alerts. Optimize can recommend batch sizes that minimize cost while meeting p99 latency.
[06:16] Priya: do you have a recommended p99 target for responsive UI?
[06:19] Ethan: for chat UI target p99 under 800ms ideally; first-token under 200-250ms is excellent. but depends on model size and prompt length. smaller models will do 1st token faster.
[06:32] Priya: can you quantify cost difference between fp16 and int8 for our workload?
[06:35] Ethan: we'd need sample prompts. we offered to run a benchmark — we typically see 30–60% lower cost on int8 depending on sequence length and kernel support. i'll run against 10 representative payloads you share.
[06:49] Aisha: what's the support SLA for Hosted?
[06:52] Maya: standard hosted support is 24x5, enterprise SLA with faster SLAs available for Dedicated/Private. we'll share the SLA doc.
[06:58] Tomás: any gotchas with streaming clients on mobile?
[07:01] Ethan: mobile clients need to handle partial tokens, reassembly, and network blips. use idempotency and consider implementing client-side ephemeral caching. also limit concurrent open streams per device.
[07:14] Priya: okay let's talk pilot shape, we want to test 2 flows: short replies (support chat) and long summaries (doc ingest). success metrics: p99 latency < 1s for support, summary quality pass at 90% of baseline.
[07:27] Maya: sounds good. next steps we'll run a perf test for both flows, share security pack and pilot pricing.
[07:33] Ethan: i'm going to run a quick demo of a retry failure — simulate gateway timeout and show idempotency dedupe. (simulates)
[07:46] Ethan: here console shows first attempt timed out at 850ms, client retried with same idempotency key; backend returned cached result, no double token charge.
[08:02] Tomás: nice. that's helpful.
[08:05] Maya: any other questions?
[08:07] Priya: just one — do you provide transcript of outputs for compliance? we need to keep traces for audits.
[08:13] Ethan: Console has request logs and optional longer retention for enterprise. Private deployments can export logs to your SIEM.
[08:21] Priya: perfect.
[08:23] Maya: recap of next steps: send security docs, run perf, schedule follow-up week of 3/24. thanks all.
[08:31] Tomás: thank you.
[08:33] Aisha: thanks.
[08:36] Maya: bye.
